Long-term Remission of Refractory Stiff-Man Syndrome After Treatment
With Intravenous Immunoglobulin
HOMA YOUN KHANLOU, MD, AND GLENN EIGER, MD
The stiff-man syndrome is a rare neuromuscular disorder
characterized by progressive rigidity, stiffness, and inter­
mittent spasm of axial and extremity muscles. Its etiology
is unknown. Different therapeutic regimens have been
used with variable success. We present a case of refractory
stiff-man syndrome, in which the symptoms were success­
fully controlled by the administration of intravenous im­
munoglobulin (IVIg). This case gives evidence that IVIg
can be a safe and an efficient treatment of refractory stiff-
T
he stiff-man syndrome (SMS) or stiff-person syn­
drome, originally described by Moersch and Wolt­
man,I is a rare neuromuscular disorder characterized by
progressive rigidity, stiffness, and intermittent spasm of
axial and extremity muscles. The etiology of SMS is un­
known, but new evidence suggests a possible autoimmune
basis.i" Up to 60% of patients with SMS may be sero­
positive for anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) anti­
bodies, an enzyme regulating the synthesis of y-amino­
butyric acid (GABA).4.5Diagnostic criteria for SMS have
been extensively reviewed by Lorish et a1.6However, many
patients do not show the classic axial distribution of stiff­
ness. Recently, Brown et al? and Barker et al" reported a
small series of patients with the stiff-limb syndrome in
whom the rigidity and spasms were confined to the distal
limbs, mainly legs, and were associated with sphincter or
brain stem involvement. It was suggested that these pa­
tients represented a distinct syndrome, probably caused by
a chronic spinal interneuritis."
Various therapeutic regimens, including diazepam,
clonazepam, baclofen, corticosteroids, and plasmapheresis
or intravenous immunoglobulin (TVlg), have been tried
with variable success.s"" We report a case of a patient who
presented with the diagnosis of SMS, whose symptoms
were successfully controlled by the administration of IVIg.
From the Department of Medicine, Albert Einstein Medical Center,
Philadelphia, Pa.
This report is dedicated to the memory of our mentor, Dr Mark
Faynberg.

effectiveness of IVIg in the treatment of this rare entity
remain to be determined.

man syndrome
REPORT OF A CASE
A 43-year-old man presented in 1997 with a 9-year history
of frequent spasms affecting both legs and neck. He had on
1 occasion been prescribed diazepam, which he did not
take. He noticed that sudden auditory (such as telephone
rings) or emotional stimuli (such as anger, fear) exagger­
ated these spasms. These episodes were absent during
sleep. Several other visits to multiple physicians did not
alleviate his symptoms despite prescriptions of drugs such
as aspirin, ibuprofen, and quinine. Continuous back rigidity
and stiffness, progressive development of back deformity,
and difficulty in ambulation secondary to the rigidity and
intermittent severe spasms of his thighs prompted this
medical visit.

Findings on his physical examination were normal ex­
cept for an exaggerated lordosis with tense contracture of
his prominent paraspinal muscles. Magnetic resonance im­
aging of the head and spinal cord was normal. His complete
blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and serum
glucose, triiodothyronine, thyroxine, thyroid-stimulating
hormone, and cortisol levels were within normal limits. An
electromyogram revealed the presence of persistent motor
unit potentials in both agonist and antagonist muscles de­
spite the patient's intention to relax, consistent with the
diagnosis of SMS.6 Furthermore, a serum anti-GAD anti­
body assay was positive. The patient was started on
diazepam with gradual increment up to 40 mg/d but had
only mild improvement of the symptoms. Baclofen, 10 mg
3 times a day, was added to the regimen without clinical
benefit. Four months later with persistent symptoms and
lack of response to diazepam and baclofen, the patient was
hospitalized and was treated with 0.4 g/kg of IVIg for 5
days, followed by 2 additional injections at a l-week inter-

val. One week after the first course of IVIg, the patient no
longer complained of muscle spasms or stiffness. Complete
resolution of rigidity and spasms followed the second and
third doses of IVIg. He remains free of such symptoms
after 2 years of follow-up.
DISCUSSION
The neurophysiologic basis of SMS remains obscure, but
recent evidence suggests an autoimmune process. In fact,
15% to 30% of these patients have clinical evidence of
other autoimmune disorders such as Hashimoto thyroid­
itis, type 1 diabetes mellitus, pernicious anemia, and
myasthenia gravis.v" About two thirds of patients have
autoantibodies directed against GAD.3,4It has been hypoth­
esized that the presence of anti-GAD antibodies may result
in the dysfunction of GAB A-mediated processes, including
the mechanisms involved in the control of muscle tone.
However, the relevance of anti-GAD in the pathogenesis of
SMS remains unresolved. In fact, the presence of anti­
GAD antibodies has been found to be associated with
other autoantibodies, such as anti-pancreatic islet cell,
anti-parietal cell, anti-smooth muscle antibodies, and anti­
microsomal, antithyroglobulin, and anti-DNA autoanti­
bodies. l-4,14-16 Moreover, GAD is an enzyme present at high
concentration in the beta cells of the pancreas, and 70% of
patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus have anti-GAD anti­
bodies.>' Despite the high incidence of anti-GAD anti­
bodies in these patients, muscle stiffness and rigidity are
rare."" Furthermore, anti-GAD antibodies are not present
in the subgroup of patients with stiff-limb syndrome or
those who have cancer. 3,7,8,17
The clinical improvement following the use of plasma­
pheresis," corticosteroids.v" and IVIg10,11 lends credence
to the probability that SMS is an autoimmune disorder, The
mechanism of immunosuppression by IVIg is unknown but
may be related to possible binding to idiotypic or Fc re­
gions of the autoantibodies.P:'? Such binding may neutral­
ize the autoantibodies. Similar binding to B cells respon­
sible for the production of the autoantibodies might result
in B-cell downregulation as well.":" Furthermore, the ad­
ministration of exogenous IgG could accelerate the rate of
pathologic endogenous IgG catabolism, presumably by
saturating maximally its protective receptor, FcRn. 19-2 1
Without this protective receptor, IgG would be degraded
by the lysosome.">'
This case gives further evidence that IVIg is a safe and
efficient regimen in the treatment of refractory SMS.
Therefore, it seems reasonable to propose IVIg treatment to
patients diagnosed as having SMS who fail to respond to
the conventional therapy of benzodiazepines or baclo­
fen.'?" However, IVIg does not constitute the ultimate

curative therapy for SMS, as relapses may occur. Further
studies are warranted to define the exact indication and the
cost-effectiveness of IVIg in the treatment of this rare
entity.
